articles.text: Piedmont community leans In Editor: The Piedmont parent community has demonstrated incredible ongoing support for our students. Last summer, our school board tapped community member and COVID expert Dr. George Rutherford to discuss safety around school opening (Thank you Dr. Rutherford for your talks to PUSD and LWV). As PUSD started planning for the 2020-2021 school year, Piedmont parents rose up. Our parent health care workers offered to hold Q&A sessions for PUSD staff on COVID transmission and safety practices initially; and most recently, vaccine safety. In preparation for our purple tier waiver application, our advocates appealed to PUSD’s insurer Kaiser Permanente to prioritize teacher testing, meet with the county supervisors’ office to clarify waiver requirements, and introduced PUSD leadership to companies providing teacher/student testing and contact tracing services. With the start of school, parents provided critical tech support for chromebook roll out. We spent countless hours collecting data from other districts, sharing best practices, and campaigning with Alameda County leadership for clear and consistent guidelines for a return to in-person learning. Despite our community’s acute increase in childcare, extracurricular, and supplemental academics expenses, the PEF volunteers worked tirelessly to ultimately fundraise at levels comparable to years pre-pandemic. Parent clubs initiated a mask fundraising with high quality masks donated to teachers, ensuring both student and teacher safety. A single Piedmont mom spearheaded the placement of HEPA filters in the classrooms. During synchronous [learning] time, we provide our children with private, quiet workspace (sometimes in the form of our home office). We have up-ended our work schedules to prevent connectivity issues. For essential workers, our children often had to navigate this process largely on their own as we could not always be home with them to help navigate a new way of learning on-line curricula or offer emotional support during periods of depression from social isolation. Unfortunately, many in our community have needed to provide additional professional mental health support for their children. Many of us reduced hours, delayed a return to the workforce, or passed up on career advancement opportunities. We all work nights and weekends because there is simply no other time. Some have left their jobs. We are all grateful to be in a position to be able to make this choice. Piedmont families, you have fully leaned in, providing time, money, skills, energy, patience and strength. Unfortunately, we cannot relent in supporting our children and their education until PUSD can also rise up.

articles.text: You may have heard about the “Immersive Van Gogh” exhibit coming to San Francisco. This West Coast premiere of a show seen by over 2 million in Paris, is billed as an “immersive” experience, because viewers wander through 300,000 cubic feet of animations, and 60,600 frames of video enhanced by 90,000,000 pixels of light, all digitizing Van Gogh’s creations. The promoters go on to promise that the astonishing scale and breathtaking creativity of the exhibit will allow one to “experience the organic landscapes of Van Gogh’s imagination and journey through his brilliance and madness.” I wonder, would Van Gogh go? It doesn’t seem all that organic if the actual paint and brush strokes are digitized. It makes me wonder whose madness we will actually be journeying through. I was taught that art is best interpreted from the inside out, not the outside in. Our technological culture often works with the premise that understanding and awareness, even meaning, comes at us, rather than emerges from within us. Don’t get me wrong, I definitely want to see this exhibit. I have never experienced 90 million pixels all at once. But I also believe that beauty, inspiration and meaning are spiritual experiences which come from within even if catalyzed from without. If I can’t perceive beauty, no amount of technological bombardment will save me. Perhaps some self-reflection is in order. I know one thing for sure. We have all had our own immersion experiences this year. The “art” in our stories of faith have come alive in new ways, not because the stories have been enhanced but because we have been immersed in some of the struggles these stories were grounded in. There is the world, but there is also our perception of the world. And our perception has changed because we were all cast into the deep end of the experiences of this year. Being in lockdown has resonated with the stories of fearful disciples locking their doors to ward off threats of their own. articles.text: Eligibility for Californians ages 50 and over opens tomorrow Expecting a huge boost in COVID-19 vaccine supply, the state announced on Thursday, March 25 that all Californians ages 16 and up will be able to make vaccination appointments starting on Thursday, April 15. People ages 50 and above will be able to make appointments starting tomorrow, Thursday, April 1. Even with the increased supply, the state expects that the vaccination of Californians who wish to be vaccinated will take several months. “With vaccine supply increasing and by expanding eligibility to more Californians, the light at the end of the tunnel continues to get brighter,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom. “We remain focused on equity as we extend vaccine eligibility to those 50 and over starting April 1, and those 16 and older starting April 15.” Last week, Alameda County opened vaccine eligibility to people aged 16 to 64 years “who are deemed to be at the very highest risk due to complex health conditions,” the county stated. The severe health conditions include cancer, kidney disease, down syndrome, pregnancy, sickle cell disease, heart conditions, severe obesity and several other comorbidities. The full list can be found on the County website at: covid-19. acgov.org/vaccines.page People aged 65 years and older have been eligible for weeks. Essential workers in healthcare, food, agriculture, education, childcare, emergency services, public transportation and air travel are eligible. Additionally, those working or living in congregate living facilities, including people experiencing homelessness, are eligible. Residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. California is encouraging residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn.ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. Over 57 percent of Piedmont’s population, some 4,760 people, has received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine as of March 29, and almost 40 percent of the City’s residents (est. 3,200) are fully vaccinated, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department. Vaccines created by Moderna and Pfizer require two doses administered several weeks apart. A recently approved vaccine manufactured by Johnson & Johnson requires only one dose, but just a few thousand doses of this vaccine have arrived in the county so far. Much more are expected to arrive in the coming days. Piedmont still leads the rest of the cities of Alameda County in terms of vaccinated population, but rates across the county have increased in recent weeks. In all of Alameda County, about 822,000 total doses have been administered and around 24 percent of the county’s population is fully vaccinated. In Oakland, about 39 percent of the population has received at least one dose and 23 percent have been fully vaccinated. articles.text: Editor: It has been more than a year into a global pandemic and more than a year in the rise of brutal attacks on Asians in America. From being gunned down in Atlanta to being beaten on the streets of San Francisco, Asians in America have been and continue to be attacked. Why does that matter? Why would that matter to us here in Piedmont? As residents of Piedmont, we pride ourselves on being educated, on being able to live in safety, on being able to raise kids that will thrive in a world where diversity is now the norm and not the exception. At a time when Asians are under attack in America, it is our goal and responsibility to ensure that Piedmont residents acknowledge what is happening in our country and to take action in our own community. The grandfather who is beaten to death. The mothers murdered. The grandmother who fought back but is left with eyes too injured to see. Those are our daughters, sons, mothers, fathers, siblings, and elders. As Asian Americans, we are wrestling with how to explain these attacks to our children and support them in the trauma they experience. How is it that people would attack us simply because of the color of our skin and the bodies we inhabit? How would you explain that to your own children? We experience the attacks of this month against the backdrop of the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, the Japanese Internment Camps during World War II, and the 1982 murder of Vincent Chin. The perpetual message is that we – Asians in America, even those born here – do not belong. Our lives are not of the same value as the lives of our white neighbors. From the irresponsible use of terms like “China Virus” and “Kung Flu” from the powerful seat of the prior president, to the claims in mainstream news that the murder of six Asian women in Atlanta last week was not racially motivated, Asians have been minimized, and erased. I am writing on behalf of members and the board of the Piedmont Asian American Club. Piedmont is a safe place, with supportive schools and organizations like the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee and the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign. articles.text: The current public health crisis has proved that there will always be a need for those who are generous enough to volunteer their time and skills. Piedmont residents have a wealth of opportunities to explore. Thanks to suggestions from residents, the Piedmont Post has compiled a list of organizations that are currently seeking volunteers. Alameda County Community Food Bank For 35 years, Alameda County Community Food Bank (ACCFB) has pursued a hunger-free community in Alameda County. ACCFB always has a need for volunteers, but at the moment, their greatest need is for weekday volunteers who can commit to joining the team weekly for full days for at least one month. You can choose to work in weekday food sorting and packaging, volunteer as a market vehicle loader, or in drivethrough distribution. Group reservations are encouraged, so grab a few friends and spend a day giving back. To learn more about volunteering, email volunteer@accfb.org. To learn more about ACCFB’s safety measures and current needs, visit https://www. accfb.org/get-involved/volunteer/. Lake Merritt Institute Lake Merritt Institute volunteers are responsible for keeping Lake Merritt clean. Because of COVID, access to “U-Clean-it” boxes around Lake Merritt are restricted to properly trained volunteers. Volunteers meet at the Institute office, on the second floor of the Boating Center at 568 Bellevue Avenue, and usually work two to three hours. Training is available from Lake Merritt Institute staff upon request by calling the office at 510-238-2290. Volunteers remove approximately 1,000 to 5,000 pounds of trash from the shores of Lake Merritt every month. Cleanup days are Tuesday at 10:30 a.m., and Saturday at 10 a.m. Numerous members of the Piedmont High Key Club can be found cleaning the lake on any given Saturday. Visit https://lakemerrittinstitute.org/ about-the-institute/ for more information about the organization. Asian Health Services Asian Health Services, located in Oakland, provides health, social, and advocacy services for all regardless of income, insurance status, immigration status, language or culture. The organization provides healthcare to more than 50,000 patients in English and over 14 Asian languages. Volunteers are critical to the center and contribute enormously to patients’ experiences. Opportunities are available in both clinical and non-clinical settings, including: health education, fundraising, language access, and administration. You must complete an online application. For more information, call (510) 986-6830 or email hr@ahschc.org. Visit https://asianhealthservices.org/volunteer-opportunities/ for more information. Project Open Hand Project Open Hand’s mission is to improve health outcomes by providing nutritious meals to the sick and vulnerable in the East Bay. Founded in 1985, the organization provides meals with love to critically ill neighbors and seniors. Each day, volunteers prepare 2,500 nutritious meals, and provide 200 bags of healthy groceries. There is also a need for volunteers, but due to COVID, volunteer shifts can be limited. If you are interested in scheduling a weekly volunteer shift, Project Open Hand asks for a 6-month commitment or 40 hours a semester for students. Contact volunteer@openhand.org with questions or to sign up. Visit https://www.openhand.org/volunteer/volunteer-alameda-county/ individual-alameda-county for more information. East Bay SPCA The East Bay’s oldest animal welfare organization is always in need of volunteers. Volunteering is a wonderful way to improve the lives of animals in the shelter, and a variety of opportunities are available for all ages. East Bay SPCA’s Humane Education programs are tailored for youth volunteers, and sessions are now open for registration. Some examples of potential service projects include making dog treats, assisting with shelter laundry, socializing with animals in the SPCA’s care, and more. Participants will learn about responsible pet care, the medical needs of animals, and pet behavior. Visit https://eastbayspca.org/whatwe-do/humane-education/shelter-scouts/ to sign up for a session. The two organizations created the Solidarity Wall so that Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders in Piedmont could feel both support and solidarity from their neighbors, Cheng explained. The groups also wanted to raise awareness to the wider community about the attacks against Asian Americans that have become more frequent in previous months, especially in the Bay Area. “We’ve heard from many Asian American youth that they don’t feel the schools or their peers understand the degree to which Asian Americans have been subjected to racism historically or in the present. We’re hoping to draw attention and spur action on antiAsian hate,” Cheng said. The nationally-observed “Stand With Asians” day was envisioned by Tian He, who was inspired to start this movement following the murder of his friend, a 36-year-old man who was stabbed multiple times in Manhattan’s Chinatown district on February 25. That murder is in addition to a slew of murders, attacks, assaults, and robberies of Asian individuals and Asian-owned businesses, mostly concentrated in New York City, San Francisco, Oakland, and Los Angeles. Last Friday, those who wanted to get involved were asked to create, produce, and post Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) awareness content. Piedmont’s Solidarity Wall served as a community call-to-action. “We’ve heard from community members that the wall has Cassindy Chao (left), Catherine Zhang, Suzy Skugstad, Judy Li, and Alana Zhou stand with signs of support at the Solidarity Wall. On Friday the Solidarity Wall began to accumulate artwork and messages from Piedmont community members in an effort spearheaded by Diana Lee and Irene Cheng. Kids gathered through the weekend at the Exedra to write notes and post signs on the Exedra. One of many posters that appeared at the Exedra. In addition to these colorful graphics with messages such as “We Belong,” people walking by the exedra created their own messages of support for the Asian community and posted them up. Diana Lee (left) co-founder of the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign, and Cassindy Chao, co-president of the Piedmont Asian American Club, co-organizers of the pop-up solidarity wall. already sparked many dialogues that may not otherwise have happened, among AAPI community, between AAPI folks and their non-AAPI friends and neighbors, between parents and children, between students and their peers, and between teachers and students. Several community members have mentioned that they found the display poignant and moving, offering a space to reflect and to process what has been happening. We hope the wall spurs further conversation, solidarity, and anti-racism efforts within our community, and beyond,” Cheng said. Residents began adorning the wall as early as 10 a.m. on Friday, March 26, and continued posting signs of support through the weekend. City Councilmember Conna McCarthy, who visited the wall on Friday to place flowers, echoed Cheng’s sentiments. “We’re in a time where everyone’s hearts are breaking because of this kind of violence. Showing up is the first step in taking responsibility for changing it,” she said. “I saw children putting flowers and writing notes, with their mothers and guardians explaining to them why this wall has to be here, and why it’s important. Our community is in a place where we can get together and make a strong statement.” Cheng said that she hopes the dialogue continues, and that Piedmonters will reach out to their Asian American neighbors, check in, and ask how they are doing. Posters produced a powerful message. The Solidarity Wall remained up at the Exedra until Sunday at 5 p.m. when the signs and artwork were taken down and transferred to Piedmont High.

articles.text: Since February, Piedmont parents have advocated for more in-person class time in their appearances at school board meetings, city-wide installation of lawn signs and through independent surveys. Currently, elementary students attend class nine hours a week, high schoolers (taking a full class load) get four hours and 22.5 minutes per week and middle schoolers attend class only two and half hours per week. With vaccinations steadily increasing and COVID cases dwindling (Alameda County is now in the orange tier), the California Department of Public Health’s revised guideline for minimum physical spacing in schools was reduced from six feet to three feet. The health directive stated three feet was “strongly recommended” as a guideline but not required. If other safety measures, like masks and air filters are in place and enforced, under three feet spacing between students is allowed by the state and Alameda County. Piedmont School District began negotiating with its the labor unions representing school administrators, classified staff and teachers on March 24, to expand in-person class time for the remainder of the Spring semester. Including the March 24 bargaining session, the district has held two negotiation sessions with teachers, totaling four and a half hours of negotiation. The content of negotiations, initial positions and statuses of negotiation have not been publicly revealed. At the March 24 school board meeting, dozens of parents called in via Zoom to push for a written confirmation by the district for 100 percent in-class instruction for next fall and an increase now in the spring. The initial discussion on the topic by the board and the ensuing public comment took nearly two and a half hours. “I’m very, very concerned and wonder why it took so long to get teachers back to the negotiating table,” said parent Leslie Santos. “You negotiated the MOU in August; no one anticipated these vaccines as early as December. The vaccines alone should have been an event special enough to start negotiations.” The current MOU created in August and amended in February is still built upon previous Covid guidelines which require six feet of space between students. That guideline has been reduced to three feet between students “We are currently in negotiations. I want to thank APT (teachers union) for coming to the table. I am confident that we will be able to come to agreements that will provide additional time for on-campus instruction, though without sacrificing opportunities for the education for those that choose to remain as Distance Learners,” Booker stated. On March 24, Booker expressed optimism that he would have news of the bargaining developments or even a new tentative agreement to share “early next week.” As of press time, no new developments have been announced. The district intends to call a special board meeting “the second we come up with tentative agreements” Booker said. In addition to coming to terms with teachers, a few logistical items stand in the way of expanding the schedule. The district still needs to conduct a new survey of families to determine who wants in-person and who wants to stay in Distance Learning. Some school sites may need to purchase new furniture (smaller desks). And the district is looking to hire additional teachers to attend to distance learners (primarily at the elementary level). Nine weeks of class remain until the last day of school, June 11.

articles.text: For some students, working with numbers and equations can be stressful. But basic math skills, like most things in life, can be achieved by anyone by following the most common-sense route: practice. Memorization of the basic math facts is critical to success in math. Memorization is not out. Basic arithmetic skills are useful for recognizing and using patterns in everyday life. Also, memorization of basic facts is necessary for success in test taking. Students who do not know basic arithmetic by memory must laboriously figure out each answer when problem solving. These students run out of time, energy and patience long before completing the test. Instead of focusing on problem-solving techniques, these students spend valuable time and energy figuring out basic math facts. If you notice your child is struggling in mathematics, consider nightly math fact “drills.” This practice is useful for students of all ages and is highly encouraged for children in kindergarten through fourth grade. Find an appropriate operation for your child’s grade level; for example, in kindergarten, students are beginning to memorize addition facts. By fourth grade, multiplication facts should be mastered. Timed tests are given for one minute, during which the student should be writing continuously. Students are expected to know answers instantly. There should be no time to think about or figure out the answer. A child should know that 3 + 4 = 7 as quickly as he or she knows that capital H goes with lower case h. A great online resource that students can work on independently is called Rocket Math. It can be downloaded onto your child’s computer or iPad by visiting play.rocketmath.com. Of course, there is always the tried-and-true option of paper and pencil: simply write a few, single-digit addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division problems for your child to solve. A short, nightly drill is recommended. Find what works best for your child, from flash cards, to computer programs, to writing the facts. At least some written practice is beneficial. Educators, and parents, know that children are motivated by mastery – and practicing basic math facts daily means more success in cumulative problem-solving. Allyson Aleksey is a former 4th grade teacher at a private, accelerated school in Metairie, Louisiana.

pages.text: 6 Wednesday, March 31, 2021 SchOOLs Teachers, school district begin negotiations for in-person class time this spring By Jay Russell Since February, Piedmont parents have advocated for more in-person class time in their appearances at school board meetings, city-wide installation of lawn signs and through independent surveys. Currently, elementary students attend class nine hours a week, high schoolers (taking a full class load) get four hours and 22.5 minutes per week and middle schoolers attend class only two and half hours per week. With vaccinations steadily increasing and COVID cases dwindling (Alameda County is now in the orange tier), the California Department of Public Health’s revised guideline for minimum physical spacing in schools was reduced from six feet to three feet. The health directive stated three feet was “strongly recommended” as a guideline but not required. If other safety measures, like masks and air filters are in place and enforced, under three feet spacing between students is allowed by the state and Alameda County. Piedmont School District began negotiating with its the labor unions representing school administrators, classified staff and teachers on March 24, to expand in-person class time for the remainder of the Spring semester. Including the March 24 bargaining session, the district has held two negotiation sessions with teachers, totaling four and a half hours of negotiation. The content of negotiations, initial positions and statuses of negotiation have not been publicly revealed. At the March 24 school board meeting, dozens of parents called in via Zoom to push for a written confirmation by the district for 100 percent in-class instruction for next fall and an increase now in the spring. The initial discussion on the topic by the board and the ensuing public comment took nearly two and a half hours. “I’m very, very concerned and wonder why it took so long to get teachers back to the negotiating table,” said parent Leslie Santos. “You negotiated the MOU in August; no one anticipated these vaccines as early as December. The vaccines alone should have been an event special enough to start negotiations.” The current MOU created in August and amended in February is still built upon previous Covid guidelines which require six feet of space between students. That guideline has been reduced to three feet between students “We are currently in negotiations. I want to thank APT (teachers union) for coming to the table. I am confident that we will be able to come to agreements that will provide additional time for on-campus instruction, though without sacrificing opportunities for the education for those that choose to remain as Distance Learners,” Booker stated. On March 24, Booker expressed optimism that he would have news of the bargaining developments or even a new tentative agreement to share “early next week.” As of press time, no new developments have been announced. The district intends to call a special board meeting “the second we come up with tentative agreements” Booker said. In addition to coming to terms with teachers, a few logistical items stand in the way of expanding the schedule. The district still needs to conduct a new survey of families to determine who wants in-person and who wants to stay in Distance Learning. Some school sites may need to purchase new furniture (smaller desks). And the district is looking to hire additional teachers to attend to distance learners (primarily at the elementary level). Nine weeks of class remain until the last day of school, June 11. TIPS FROM A TEACHER In math, memorization is not “out” By Allyson Aleksey For some students, working with numbers and equations can be stressful. But basic math skills, like most things in life, can be achieved by anyone by following the most common-sense route: practice. Memorization of the basic math facts is critical to success in math. Memorization is not out. Basic arithmetic skills are useful for recognizing and using patterns in everyday life. Also, memorization of basic facts is necessary for success in test taking. Students who do not know basic arithmetic by memory must laboriously figure out each answer when problem solving. These students run out of time, energy and patience long before completing the test. Instead of focusing on problem-solving techniques, these students spend valuable time and energy figuring out basic math facts. If you notice your child is struggling in mathematics, consider nightly math fact “drills.” This practice is useful for students of all ages and is highly encouraged for children in kindergarten through fourth grade. Find an appropriate operation for your child’s grade level; for example, in kindergarten, students are beginning to memorize addition facts. By fourth grade, multiplication facts should be mastered. Timed tests are given for one minute, during which the student should be writing continuously. Students are expected to know answers instantly. There should be no time to think about or figure out the answer. A child should know that 3 + 4 = 7 as quickly as he or she knows that capital H goes with lower case h. A great online resource that students can work on independently is called Rocket Math. It can be downloaded onto your child’s computer or iPad by visiting play.rocketmath.com. Of course, there is always the tried-and-true option of paper and pencil: simply write a few, single-digit addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division problems for your child to solve. A short, nightly drill is recommended. Find what works best for your child, from flash cards, to computer programs, to writing the facts. At least some written practice is beneficial. Educators, and parents, know that children are motivated by mastery – and practicing basic math facts daily means more success in cumulative problem-solving. Allyson Aleksey is a former 4th grade teacher at a private, accelerated school in Metairie, Louisiana. articles.text: As Piedmont High School’s campus transitions to incorporate a new STEAM building and theater, the question was asked, “What would make it more ideal?” A panel of students, faculty, administration, parents and community members invested hours into deliberating this very question. It was especially noted that while students were performing at remarkably high levels, there certainly was an opportunity for their learning experiences to provide more joy and real-world relevance. Students can too easily view their high school years as only a hoop that must be jumped through, so that one day – perhaps years in the future – they might make a difference in the world and be able to enjoy their contributions to it. Expo has been designed to seize the opportunity to make high school a more joyful and relevant experience. Expo will allow students to apply their knowledge and skills from all of their learning experiences to a problem in which they bring their own passion and interest. For Expo, students will research and analyze a problem of their choosing and persuasively reveal their proposed solution to the world at the culminating Expo event. The manner and form of what students produce for an Expo project is limitless. One might design a tangible object in the STEAM building engineering lab or at home, or the project may be a policy proposal. It could be a book, a song, a computer program, a widget, a business venture, an academic course, an automobile, a sensor, an analyzer, a TED Talk, an Eagle Scout project, or almost anything. It might be geared locally, regionally, nationally or globally. It might completely eradicate a problem, or it might simply serve to contribute in a meaningful way towards mitigation of the problem. All student projects will be revealed at the Expo event on June 4 at 7 p.m., and top tier projects will be highlighted. Judges will identify top tier projects utilizing the rubric included in the Expo Student Guide, available at tinyurl.com/piedmontexpo. It’s important to remember that the Expo project is a standalone work, guided by each individual student’s discretion. Several teachers have incorporated a portion, or even all of their final assessment, as a demonstration of proficiency in standards that could possibly be fully met while students are working on their Expo project. Many student questions are answered in the Student Guide, but clarification is available by e-mailing Mr. Christensen at fchristensen@piedmont.k12. ca.us. articles.text: Some children push their tongue between their front teeth when swallowing, eating, talking, or while at rest. This is called tongue thrust. It is normal (and protective) for infants to hold their tongues forward when they swallow, but this pattern should stop by the time your child is about 1½ years old. Our tongue stays behind our teeth when we speak, not visible to the listener, with the exception of the “th” sound. However, if your child has a tongue thrust, you may see his tongue when he speaks or eats. Since a tongue thrust can also push your child’s teeth out of place, your child’s dentist may be the first person to tell you that the tongue thrust is causing a problem. Where should our tongue be? The normal posture is to rest the tongue up on the roof of the mouth, about ½ an inch away from the front teeth. Lips should be closed, and teeth slightly apart. Tongue thrust can be caused by a narrowed airway which results in mouth breathing because of allergies or large tonsils. Tongue thrust can be caused by prolonged thumb sucking, or pacifier, bottle or sippy cup use that may change the shape of your child’s jaw, palate and teeth. Tongue thrust can also be due to tongue or lip weakness, or developmental delays. Tongue thrust can be related to a tongue tie. Tongue thrust can also have a Tongue thrusting can lead to many problems. genetic component. The constant improperly placed pressure generated by the tongue thrust can create problems with dental health, speech and the cosmetic appearance of the face over time. We swallow approximately 2,000 times per day with the tongue generating up to 4 pounds of pressure per swallow. Tongue thrust can occur throughout the lifespan. For the infant and very young child, trouble latching, persistent drooling and messy eating may be evident. For the school aged child, dental and speech issues such as a lisp may be noted. Tongue thrust can also cause orthodontic relapse if untreated. In adulthood, sleep disordered breathing, TMJ and facial pain can present. Treatment of tongue thrust usually involves multiple disciplines. Dentists can address the associated oral health issues. Orthodontists can treat the resultant misalignment of the teeth and jaw. While the dentist and orthodontist treat problems which have already occurred, a therapist can correct the tongue thrust problem and the habit at the root of the issue to prevent further complications and promote long term success with your orthodontic investments. Therapy can re-train the muscles of the face and tongue for proper posture at rest, as well as during speech and swallowing. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. articles.text: Deadline to enter League of Women Voters contest is April 17 The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is sponsoring its second annual essay contest, open to all Piedmont high school juniors and seniors. The essay should answer the question, “Given the fragility of democracy as evidenced by the insurrection of January 6, 2021, how can your generation work to ensure that democracy in the United States is strengthened for future generations?” Contest entrants may, but are not required to, rely on outside sources that are properly cited within the text and in a bibliography. A specific format for citations or bibliography is not required, but there must be enough information to allow the judges to easily verify your sources. Citations do not count toward your total number of words. Remember that this essay is not solely a research paper and should draw on the writer’s personal experiences and insights. Essays will be judged on originality, clarity of expression, vocabulary and style, proper grammar, punctuation and spelling. Students are encouraged to have a teacher, parent or mentor review the essay prior to submission keeping in mind that all work must be the student’s own. The essay must be 250 to 500 words, excluding citations. At the top of the essay include the following information: the title, your first and last name, city of residence (must be Piedmont), name of your school, and your current grade. articles.text: Brian Cain runs for 229 yards, 4 TDs Photos by Todd Marshburn Piedmont running back Brian Cain had a career day on Saturday, running for 229 yards and four touchdowns against Mt. Eden. Piedmont’s football team traveled to Hayward on Saturday, March 27, where, behind a monster game by sunning back Brian Cain, it obliterated the Mt. Eden Monarchs, 42-7. Cain, a senior, ran for 229 yards and scored four touchdowns. “It was the most rushing yards I’ve ever had. We knew that once we’d get to the second-level of their defense, their larger linebackers wouldn’t be able to chase us down,” said Cain. The Highlanders led 28-7 by halftime, and Cain already had three touchdowns. But it was Piedmont’s defense that quickly figured out the Monarchs’ offense and its mobile quarterback, Alejandro Villanueva, He had more than 20 run attempts, but was held to 70 yards. The Monarchs were coming off a 48-32 win against Newark Memorial where Villanueva was the bulk of their offense. “I didn’t think we’d blow them out like that. We knew that he was a critical piece of their offense. He had big windows to throw against Newark Memorial, and there’s a big difference when you apply pressure,” explained PHS coach Jerome Johnson. Piedmont’s offense plan was to stay on the ground, continuously pounding the defensive line with a healthy mix of carries to the interior line and off the edge. “We knew that they had some bigger players which didn’t really translate well to their speed. Our Offensive Coordinator Jarmar Julian told me to hit the hole and try making something out of it once you turn up field,” said Cain. After forcing a Mt. Eden punt on the opening possession, Piedmont scored on an eight-play series that capped off with a 14-yard touchdown run by Jack Nelson with 4:53 left in the first quarter. Mt. Eden responded with a 58-yard drive to tie the game at 7-7 with 1:17 seconds. Its drive included eight straight carries by its quarterback. But after that, Piedmont’s defense clamped down, limiting the Monarchs to 2-for-9 on third downs and 0-for-2 on fourth downs. Piedmont’s next score came quickly after Ben Marshburn returned the kickoff to the 40-yard line. Cain ran 16 yards off the edge, then an 18-yard carry up the gut to the six-yard line. He finished the drive with a six-yard TD for a 14-7 lead with 18 seconds left in the first quarter. PHS’ next touchdown took just two plays early in the second quarter. Starting at their own 49-yard line, Cain broke a 15-yard run off the right-edge, then followed up with a 36-yard touchdown run, breaking two tackles on his way to the end zone. Piedmont made it 28-7 after converting a 3rd-and-18 with a draw carry to Cain for 25 yards. He hurdled a low tackle attempt and spun off another defender – just part of the Cain power game. He later scored on a five-yard carry with 6:06 left in the half. Nelson got another score for the Highlanders in the third quarter on a 10-yard carry, while Cain scored his fourth touchdown on an 11-yard run in the fourth quarter. Final stats include: Cain’s 25 carries for 229 yards to average 9.16 yards per carry and four touchdowns, to go along with three tackles on defense. Nelson had five carries for 39 yards and two touchdowns. Receiver Ben Marshburn had four receptions for 47 yards and one carry for 19 yards. Defensively, linebacker Jet Moxley had seven total tackles, one for a loss of yards. LB Joe Hempeck also had seven tackles; DL Andy Melian had five total tackles and three tackles for loss; DL Mason Kimball had three tackles and one sack; Nelson had four tackles, one sack, and two tackles for loss. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-0) heads to Berkeley on Friday, April 2 for a 7:00 p.m. game. Jet Moxley (36) had seven total tackles including one for a loss.

With the sound of various birds, critters rustling in the shrubbery, and moths being awoken by my arrival, the entire trail had little evidence of being touched by man. To begin your hike, park on Moller Ranch Drive and take the Moller Ranch Trail until you reach an unlocked gate, which will take you off the paved surface and towards the canyon. Diablo of Concord to the rolling hills of Del Valle Regional Park and onto Tehan Canyon Road, which is a dirt road that borders some private ranches. Continue down the dirt road for a half mile until you reach a moss covered tree that has a large tank surrounded by a gate on the left. Once entering the canyon, the amount of lush green vegetation surrounding you is breathtaking. Everywhere you look are clovers, ferns, and moss covering every tree and rock in sight. In addition to the abundance of plants, birds of many types were flying and cawing overhead including hawks, pigeons, jays, Ferns shoot out from the hillside in Tehan Canyon. crows, and others I could not identify. articles.text: The social impact of COVID-19 on the world of sports continues to take its toll. The California Interscholastic Federation announced recently that they will be adding two new activities to its sports calendar: Birding—Bird Watching, and eSports—online gaming. Both will be added to the CIF’s Season 2 of sports starting on April 17 in order to allow more activities capable of adequate social distancing. “We’ve built a reputation for making strange decisions,” said a CIF executive who was not permitted to speak publicly. “The impact of COVID-19 on California’s prep sports seems ever-lasting and this topic has been on our desk for a while now. We feel that adding Bird Watching provides a competitive route for more students to enjoy the outdoors. Meanwhile, eSports and online gaming leagues are a well-documented growing multi-billion dollar industry. We feel these two activities will enable a demographic of non-athletic students in the larger world of sports.” In a unique breakthrough for CIF-governed prep sports in the state, students signing up for Birding or eSports will be able to compete on other school sports teams at the same time. The initial season of bird watching (birding) will get started on May 8 in conjunction with World Migratory Bird Day and run through the summer until December 31. “It’s a long season said Jason Parrot, but it follows the American Birding Association rules toward accomplishing a “Big Year.” For those not in the know, a Big Year is a challenge amongst birders to identify as many birds as possible by sight or sound within a calendar year. Members of the Class of 2021 will still be eligible to log their Big Year. Per ABA rules, the CIF will start its first full Bird Watching season on January 1, 2022 at 12:00 a.m., going for a full year until 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 31, 2022. “We realize the typical jock may not be into Bird Watching, but students interested in ornithology, biology, and environmental sciences will. Members from graduating classes will still be able to log their numbers and compete as long as their Big Year started during their high school academic career,” said the CIF. Online gaming (eSports) Online gaming will have obvious demand amongst students throughout California from Day 1. With the eSports industry valued at over $150 billion, many colleges like Ohio State, University of Texas, and UC Irvine are reported to be offering degrees in competitive gaming and video game design. In fact, organizations like www.HighSchoolEsportsLeague. com gained accreditation from STEM (Science, Technology, Education, Match), an educational research credentialing firm. They ruled that eSports is a problem-solving, team building exercise and therefore capable of hosting interscholastic competition. It is worth mentioning that Piedmont High is actually among the only schools in Alameda County not signed up for the HighSchoolEsportsLeague. High school programs which compete with PHS are already battling online, including Head-Royce, Skyline, Oakland Military Institute, Miramonte, Alameda, Encinal, San Leandro, Albany, Hayward, Castro Valley, Moreau, and Redwood Christian, according to the official HSEL website. “High Schools throughout California have already formed competitive gaming teams and competing in high-level tournaments; it really was only a matter of time,” said another CIF executive. The CIF’s initial gaming season will get started on May 1 until June 4 with EA Sports’ mainline hits Madden 21 and Fifa 21, while Epic Games’ popular classic, Fortnite, is expected to have multiple divisions. A new slate of games will be planned for the Fall of 2021. None of this is to be taken seriously, even though it is one day ahead of April Fool’s Day.

articles.text: Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) is hosting a live discussion this Saturday, April 3, entitled “Trouble in Mind: an A.C.T. Audience Exchange.” Speakers will discuss Alice Childress’ new play, Trouble in Mind., the first of American Conservatory Theatre’s (A.C.T.) “Out Loud” series featuring play readings of great playwrights from generations past. Childress’ comedy would have been the first play by a Black woman on Broadway if she had “agreed to the producers’ demands to soften its message,” the playwright explained. articles.text: San Francisco Symphony announced on March 14 that its recording of “From the Diary of Anne and Meditations on Rilke” won a 2021 Grammy award in the category of Best Classical Compendium. The album is a recording of Michael Tilson Thomas’ own compositions, featuring Isabel Leonard, Sasha Cooke, and Ryan McKinny as soloists. It was recorded live at Davies Symphony Hall in November 2018 and January 2020 and represents the first San Francisco Symphony media release of MTT’s original compositions. The concept for the album is based on the historic diary kept by Anne Frank during the height of the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. “From the Diary of Anne Frank” was commissioned by the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and originally written for Audrey Hepburn, who was a UNICEF ambassador. It received its premiere with MTT and the New World Symphony in 1990. San Francisco Symphony first performed “From the Diary of Anne Frank” in November 2018, in concerts commemorating the 70th anniversary of UNICEF’s Declaration of Human Rights, with Isabel Leonard as narrator. This marks the 16th Grammy award for the San Francisco Symphony. Since his tenure, Michael Tilson Thomas has received numerous awards and recording honors; his first recording with the symphony, Prokofiev’s Romeo and Juliet, won a 1997 Grammy. San Francisco Media is the Symphony’s in-house media production company and label, launched in 2001. Since its inception, the label has earned nine Grammy awards. All San Francisco Symphony Media recordings and videos are available online at https:// www.warnerclassics.com/artist/ Michael Tilson Thomas san-francisco-symphony/releases. “From the Diary of Anne Frank and Meditations on Rilke” is available on various platforms, including iTunes and Amazon.

articles.text: Richard Sharp and Shailene Woodley in Adrift. Movie review by Chris Honoré Before you see Adrift, resist the temptation to learn anything about the story or the overwhelming events that frame act three. The narrative is two stories. The first is a love story between two kindred spirits, Tami Oldham (Shailene Woodley) and Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin). Both twenty-something. The year is 1983. The place Tahiti. Tami, who left her home in San Diego right out of high school, began to drift from port to port throughout the South Pacific, working odd jobs, crewing on boats and tourist ships. She is newly arrived in Tahiti when she meets New Zealander, Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin), having just arrived on his trim 36-foot schooner, the Mayaluga. Almost immediately they begin a relationship, nurtured by the gorgeous beaches, long sails on Richard’s boat, strolls through outdoor marketplaces, awash in color, easy-does-it people. All is kissed by soft trade winds gently blowing through. The two relish being together, their carefree lives, while sharing a world view that takes them out and about while embracing an existence far off the grid. Richard asks Tami to join him in his travels and they plan their sail from Tahiti to places east. But unexpectedly, Richard meets two fellow sailors from London who propose to hire him to sail their spectacular boat, with all the possible comforts available on a 45- footer, from Tahiti to San Diego. The offer is sweetened with $10,000 and two first-class plane tickets back to Tahiti after the boat is delivered. The money, Tami and Richard conclude, could keep them sailing for at least a year, and so they decide to leave the Mayaluga in Tahiti and make the trip. And so begins act three, which is the most intense part of the film, but also something I will avoid mentioning in this review. This is a compellingly entertaining film, especially well-acted by Shailene Woodley who is most convincing, not only in her connection to Richard when they are in Tahiti, but her all-in performance in act three. Full disclosure: I love sailing movies. I love the idea of sails filled with wind and the absolute silence, other than the sound of halyards banging softly against the mast, or waves hitting the bow and sending up a welcoming spray that reaches the cockpit. I spent a lot of time doing all of the above on the San Francisco Bay, out by Alcatraz, and over by Tiburon, with Sausalito in the distance. But there is a caveat: blue water sailing is profoundly different and requires a sustained diligence that acknowledges the full measure of the sea and its power. Which Adrift graphically conveys. Adrift. Directed by Baltasar Kormakur. Starring Shailene Woodley and Richard Sharp. 2 hrs. Rated: PG-13.

articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré The Zookeeper’s Wife, based on the 2007 best-selling work of nonfiction by Diane Ackerman, opens with an idyllic series of images. Antonina Zabinski (Jessica Chastain) is lounging on a sun-splashed bed with two sleeping lion cubs that she holds and nuzzles. We soon see her opening the gates to a zoo, which she and her husband own. Jan (Johan Heldenbergh) welcomes families to enter and enjoy what is the equivalent of a peaceful, self-contained ark, an island of enchantment. Later, she rides her bicycle through the zoo, followed by a young camel, while she happily checks on the animals. The year is 1939. The city is Warsaw. But abruptly, Antonina’s life is upended, first with an air raid when explosions rock the zoo, killing many animals and telegraphing what is coming next: the German army has rolled into Poland and will occupy not only Warsaw but the zoo as well. The animals must go, she and Jan are told by Herman Goering’s zoologist, Lutz Heck (Daniel Bruhl), a man who, as it turns out, is a Nazi first and proves to be a danger to Antonina. Soon the couple learns that all of Warsaw is occupied and the city’s Jews had been rounded up and confined to what became known as the Warsaw Ghetto. Though the Zabinskis are gentiles and allowed to live within the zoo’s gates, many of their close friends are Jews. The Zookeeper’s Wife is told from the point of view of Antonina, and it is through her eyes that we see her struggle to comprehend the unnecessary cruelty of the occupiers. There is one scene where soldiers shoot an elephant as well as the young camel, taking great pleasure in the moment. Of course, Jan is also filled with rage at what the soldiers have done to the zoo where they had housed for years their lovingly cared-for animals. But in his travels he is exposed to the remorselessness of the Germans, realizing that what he is witnessing extends far beyond the zoo. He knows evil when he confronts it. There is a scene where he is watching small, trusting children and their terrified parents herded onto railroad cars, headed for concentration camps. It’s heart-rending. And it is at that moment that the Zabinskis make a life-changing decision. Their existential choice was to smuggle Jews from the ghetto to the zoo. The journey, while short, under the guise of collecting kitchen garbage for the zoo’s pigs, is harrowing and fraught with danger. Many of the Jews who they rescue are hidden in the basement of their home. Others are quickly trucked out of Poland. What Jan and Antonina did transcends the word “courageous.” They risked their lives while hiding Jews in what was once a sanctuary for animals and is now used as a completely different kind of haven. It’s actually a wonderful metaphor, and it’s all accomplished while surrounded by German soldiers. In the film this choice occurs quietly, absent any spoken deliberations or hesitation, with a kind of fearful fearlessness. I can only assume that for them it was a crossroads of sorts; history has shown that others did not do what the Zabinskis chose to do. They were, in most respects, ordinary people who did something extraordinary. In 1965 Israel honored them for their courage as “Righteous Ones.” They were two among those few across Europe who stepped forward while so much of the world remained silent. One last point: The Zookeeper’s Wife is, of course, a story about the holocaust. But the horror that this time represented is touched upon indirectly. While there are scenes from the Warsaw Ghetto that are breathtakingly tragic and ultimately inexplicable, it was not the intent of director Niki Caro to make a film that illustrated the graphic malevolence brought to bear by the Nazis. Films such as Night and Fog, Shoah, and Schindler’s List do this superbly. What Caro does is tell a very personal story about small acts of courage that in the aggregate were beyond heroic. It is to her credit that she found the book and enlisted Jessica Chastain, who gives a remarkable performance, to help her tell the story. The Zookeeper’s Wife. Directed by Niki Caro. Starring Jessica Chastain, Johan Heldenbergh and Daniel Bruhl. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from The Zookeeper’s Wife.

Starring Jessica Chastain, Johan Heldenbergh and Daniel Bruhl. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG-13. Richard Sharp and Shailene Woodley in Adrift. Movie review by Chris Honoré Before you see Adrift, resist the temptation to learn anything about the story or the overwhelming events that frame act three. The narrative is two stories. The first is a love story between two kindred spirits, Tami Oldham (Shailene Woodley) and Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin). Both twenty-something. The year is 1983. The place Tahiti. Tami, who left her home in San Diego right out of high school, began to drift from port to port throughout the South Pacific, working odd jobs, crewing on boats and tourist ships. She is newly arrived in Tahiti when she meets New Zealander, Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin), having just arrived on his trim 36-foot schooner, the Mayaluga. Almost immediately they begin a relationship, nurtured by the gorgeous beaches, long sails on Richard’s boat, strolls through outdoor marketplaces, awash in color, easy-does-it people. All is kissed by soft trade winds gently blowing through. The two relish being together, their carefree lives, while sharing a world view that takes them out and about while embracing an existence far off the grid. Richard asks Tami to join him in his travels and they plan their sail from Tahiti to places east. But unexpectedly, Richard meets two fellow sailors from London who propose to hire him to sail their spectacular boat, with all the possible comforts available on a 45- footer, from Tahiti to San Diego. The offer is sweetened with $10,000 and two first-class plane tickets back to Tahiti after the boat is delivered. The money, Tami and Richard conclude, could keep them sailing for at least a year, and so they decide to leave the Mayaluga in Tahiti and make the trip. And so begins act three, which is the most intense part of the film, but also something I will avoid mentioning in this review. This is a compellingly entertaining film, especially well-acted by Shailene Woodley who is most convincing, not only in her connection to Richard when they are in Tahiti, but her all-in performance in act three. Full disclosure: I love sailing movies. I love the idea of sails filled with wind and the absolute silence, other than the sound of halyards banging softly against the mast, or waves hitting the bow and sending up a welcoming spray that reaches the cockpit. I spent a lot of time doing all of the above on the San Francisco Bay, out by Alcatraz, and over by Tiburon, with Sausalito in the distance. But there is a caveat: blue water sailing is profoundly different and requires a sustained diligence that acknowledges the full measure of the sea and its power. Which Adrift graphically conveys. Adrift. Directed by Baltasar Kormakur. Starring Shailene Woodley and Richard Sharp. 2 hrs. Rated: PG-13. A scene from The Zookeeper’s Wife.

articles.text: A scene from Disney’s Moana. Review by Chris Honoré Moana is a family friendly animated feature by Disney. It is a Polynesian story about a strongwilled, adventurous girl named Moana (Auli’i Cravalho), 16, the daughter of her tribe’s chief, Tui (Temuera Morrison). Set on the pacific island of Motunui, an emerald paradise, the story begins with Moana, looking toward the horizon, ever curious, wondering what’s beyond, understanding that for years her tribe has been afraid to venture past the reef that surrounds the island. But a strange cloud now hangs over the island. The fish are not as plentiful and the coconuts dry and tasteless. Moana’s grandmother, Tala (Rachel House), tells her that the ocean has chosen her to return the island’s goddess, Te Fifi, an idol stolen by the demigod, Maui (Dwayne Johnson), a millennia ago. Late at night, in the pale moonlight, Moana takes a beached canoe, a camakan, and sets out beyond the reef in search of the hulking, overly confident demigod Maui. Her mission is to break the spell cast over her people. Moana is clearly Disney’s attempt to feature a young woman who does not need to be rescued by a prince, an almost iconic story line. Instead, the studio approaches the character of Moana with a light hand, the inherent feminism subtle but compelling. Moana is independent, courageous and never burdened with an oppressive patriarchy. It is her destiny to become the eventual chief of her tribe. There is also no love story, no rugged islander waiting to marry her. Moana is simply a story of an empowered teenage girl on a quest. The directors of the film, John Musker and Ron Clemens (The Little Mermaid, Aladdin) consulted with South Pacific locals, regarding their history and folklore. They also cast a wide net in search of the Hawaiian teen Auli’i Cravalho as the voice of Moana. As well, Dwayne Johnson, adding star power, has Samoan heritage. Voicing Moana’s father, chief Tui, is New Zealander Temuera Morrison of Maori background. Know as well that Moana is sprinkled with 10 songs, sung by Moana and Maui (as it turns out, Johnson has a solid voice) and written by Lin-Manuel Miranda of Hamilton fame. Plus, the animation is rich in tropical colors. Moana. Animation by Disney. Directed by John Musker and Ron Clemens. Voices of Auli’i Cravalho, Dwayne Johnson and Rachel House. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Swedish soprano Jenny Lind Life in the American Wild West of the mid-1800s was difficult. Americans were open to almost anything. But what they craved more than anything else was culture. They were starved for entertainment. The great showman PT Barnum saw this as a great opportunity, and he took advantage of the situation. He had heard of the famous Swedish soprano Jenny Lind, so he contacted her and proposed a concert tour in America. He added – none too subtly – that she would reap a fortune. A contract was signed and Barnum got to work doing what he did best. Jenny Lind’s name became instantly famous throughout the entire country. The year was 1852. She toured throughout the U.S., especially in the Wild West. Americans loved her. There is even a California town named Jenny Lind in the Gold Rush country, one of the many places where she performed concerts. In one year alone, she earned $350,000. That was a tremendous amount in those days. But Barnum, being Barnum, netted $500,000. That was OK because Barnum delivered the publicity and Lind delivered the entertainment. Everybody was happy. Remembering violinist Henri Vieuxtemps But Jenny Lind was not the first great musician to concertize in the Wild West. The first great artist of any note was the Belgian violinist Henri Vieuxtemps. Concerts were a lot different in those days. Almost all of them were variety shows or vaudeville shows with one or two instrumentalists and one or two singers. Some shows even had a poet added to the showbill. Appearing as the co-star with Vieuxtemps was the equally famous European pianist Sigmund Thalberg. As you can imagine, American audiences were not very sophisticated in their knowledge of music. So, the musical stars played some classical music, but they also performed popular music which Belgian violinist Henri Vieuxtemps American pianist Louis Moreau Gottschalk Norwegian violinist Ole Bull catered to the common man. One of Vieuxtemps’ famous pieces was his version of the Arkansas Traveler. Another was his version of Yankee Doodle Dandy. This was standard fare on the concert stage in the mid- 1800s, and the American public loved it all. Most of the well-publicized musicians came from Europe, but America did have one really great star. Louisiana-born Louis Moreau Gottschalk, a pianist. Barnum offered to promote concerts for Gottschalk, but the musician would have nothing to do with the razzle-dazzle style of promotion for which Barnum was noted. Gottschalk chose to do his own promotion, and he was a fabulous success everywhere he went. Unfortunately, his career was ruined by a trumped-up sex scandal. He was concertizing in San Francisco and took the ferry across the Bay to Oakland. He and a friend went to see some girls in Oakland, and that innocent event was blown into a scandal. Gottschalk barely evaded the vigilantes and fled to South America. His death was truly dramatic. Knowing that he was dying, he went to the piano one last time and played one of his famous compositions, titled Morte. He died mid-performance. The music of Ole Bull I have saved one of the most colorful characters for the end of this article. If Arnold

articles.text: The popular annual Piedmont Art Walk, now in its 2nd year, is benefitting from its success last year. To date, more than 40 local artists have registered to display their art outside on Sunday, May 2 between 12:00-5:00 p.m. Paintings, ceramics, mixed media, sculpture, and photography will be displayed and shown by local artists in front of their homes The community is invited to enjoy this outdoor art event and fundraiser hosted by local Piedmont artists and the Piedmont Arts Fund. Purchases support artists in town, and 20 percent of proceeds will be donated to the Piedmont Arts Fund to support art in the schools. This fundraising event brings together live art, artists, and community members while following Alameda County’s COVID-19 guidelines to keep everyone safe. The event is spread out over Piedmont to avoid crowds and ensure social distancing. When the COVID quarantine took effect in last March, the Piedmont Arts Fund (formerly PAINTS and CHIME) had to cancel their spring fundraisers. The diminished school budget outlook for next school year makes this year’s fundraising critical for maintaining robust art programs in Piedmont schools. The Art Walk features a Who’s Who of Piedmont artists (see list on the website), and residents and students may not realize how many accomplished artists live in Piedmont. Plan now to take a walk on Sunday afternoon, May 2 to visit the artists during the second Annual Piedmont Art Walk. Who knows? You may find a new art piece that brightens your day and supports art in the schools. For more information and to see a gallery of artists, visit https://piedmontartsfund.org/ piedmont-art-walk-2021
articles.title: List of artists grows for Piedmont Art Walk on May 2

articles.text: Charismatic Gerard Bertrand is a leading figure in the resurgence of the wines of Southern France. The Languedoc-Roussillon area in southwest France is the largest wine producing region in the world. They make more wine there than the entire United States. Unfortunately, for many years, most of it wasn’t very good. Much of it was sold in bulk and farmers were paid by the ton. The emphasis was on quantity rather than quality. After a visit to the region this summer and the chance to taste many of the region’s wines I am happy to report that the wine scene in the Languedoc is now very different. Many producers are now bottling their own wines with their name on the label and are striving mightily to improve quality. You can see the pride on their faces as they pour their wine and watch the surprise on the face of the taster who is not expecting much from a Languedoc wine. The region now seems to rival the Rhone valley in producing great wines from Syrah, Grenache, Carignan and Mourvedre. Thankfully prices have not caught up with the surge in quality and the wines remain great values in a world filled with overpriced wines. In this column and next month’s column I will be exploring and sharing some of these interesting wines with the readers. Today I want to introduce one producer who stands head and shoulders above others in terms of quality and innovation. Gerard Bertrand was born into a wine-making family with his father owning a property in the appellation of Corbierres. His early passion was rugby and he spent some time playing professionally but eventually the call of the vines overcame sports and he began developing several wine properties in the area of Narbonne and also in Roussillon. One by one he kept expanding his holdings and adding other wineries to his portfolio. Eventually he had the opportunity to purchase Chateau L’Hospitalet, a wine estate south of Narbonne in the heart of the La Clape Massif conservation area overlooking the Mediterranean Sea. There are 1,000 hectares of pine trees and vines and the estate includes a charming hotel, art gallery and exquisite gourmet restaurant. The estate also hosts a wildly popular jazz festival each summer that brings hordes of people to the property. Bertrand’s latest project is to create a “first growth” quaity wine – the Lafite of the Languedoc. He found a plot of land while hiking the La Liviniere area of Minervois, which seemed a perfect place to build a small modern, ultra high quality winery with no expense spared – thus Clos d’Ora was born. This fall they are celebrating their fourth vintage. pages.text: Wednesday, March 31, 2021 23 The Wine Corner Discovering Languedoc – the wines of Gerard Bertrand Charismatic Gerard Bertrand is a leading figure in the resurgence of the wines of Southern France. By Pierre DuMont The Languedoc-Roussillon area in southwest France is the largest wine producing region in the world. They make more wine there than the entire United States. Unfortunately, for many years, most of it wasn’t very good. Much of it was sold in bulk and farmers were paid by the ton. The emphasis was on quantity rather than quality. After a visit to the region this summer and the chance to taste many of the region’s wines I am happy to report that the wine scene in the Languedoc is now very different. Many producers are now bottling their own wines with their name on the label and are striving mightily to improve quality. You can see the pride on their faces as they pour their wine and watch the surprise on the face of the taster who is not expecting much from a Languedoc wine. The region now seems to rival the Rhone valley in producing great wines from Syrah, Grenache, Carignan and Mourvedre. Thankfully prices have not caught up with the surge in quality and the wines remain great values in a world filled with overpriced wines. In this column and next month’s column I will be exploring and sharing some of these interesting wines with the readers. Today I want to introduce one producer who stands head and shoulders above others in terms of quality and innovation. Gerard Bertrand was born into a wine-making family with his father owning a property in the appellation of Corbierres. His early passion was rugby and he spent some time playing professionally but eventually the call of the vines overcame sports and he began developing several wine properties in the area of Narbonne and also in Roussillon. One by one he kept expanding his holdings and adding other wineries to his portfolio. Eventually he had the opportunity to purchase Chateau L’Hospitalet, a wine estate south of Narbonne in the heart of the La Clape Massif conservation area overlooking the Mediterranean Sea. There are 1,000 hectares of pine trees and vines and the estate includes a charming hotel, art gallery and exquisite gourmet restaurant. The estate also hosts a wildly popular jazz festival each summer that brings hordes of people to the property. Bertrand’s latest project is to create a “first growth” quaity wine – the Lafite of the Languedoc. He found a plot of land while hiking the La Liviniere area of Minervois, which seemed a perfect place to build a small modern, ultra high quality winery with no expense spared – thus Clos d’Ora was born. This fall they are celebrating their fourth vintage. Like all of Gerard’s properties, the farming is done by the principles of Biodynamics – a philosophy of farming (and of life) that is growing rapidly in popularity in many wine regions around the world. The philosophy eschews The vines of Minervois from the Mount D’Ora winery. Working the vines of Mount D’Ora with mule and plow – Biodynamics at work. chemicals and pesticides and uses all natural methods to nurture the vines. At Clos d’Ora that includes using a mule instead of a tractor to till the soil. Planting and harvesting are done according to the movements of the stars and tides. Alongside the powerful presence of the biodynamic philosophy, the other aspect of Bertrand’s winemaking style that was powerfully evident is a meticulous, perfectionist’s attention to detail – especially cleanliness. I have visited a lot of wineries and bottling facilities in my time, but this was the first time everyone had to don white disposable lab coats to tour the plant. The size of the main facility is enormous and he makes a staggering number of wines. The wines described below are my favorites from his vast portfolio and are available online at Wine.com. from a blend of Syrah and Carignan, this wine is drinking perfectly now but also has the tannin and structure to last at least a decade. It reminds me of a baby Hermitage. • 2013 Chateau de Villemajou Grand Vin Corbieres Boutenac, $40 This is the estate Gerard Bertrand’s father bought in 1970 and the place where Gerard got his start in making wine. The wine is a mix of Carignan, Grenache, Syrah and Mourvedre. It has an intense, perfumed nose of violets and anise and tons of plum and cassis flavors in the mouth. It is a largescale wine but balanced, and will be best after a few years in the cellar. • 2015 Gris Blanc, $14 At first glance you could mis take this for a white wine. It is the palest rose I have ever seen. Made from the Grenache Gris grape, it has an enchanting nose of strawberries and wildflowers with soft peach fruit on the palate. It is crisp, dry and tremendously refreshing. The perfect summer quaffer. • 2014 Clos D’Ora, $220 There is no doubt about this being the first growth of the Languedoc. It is lovingly handcrafted from Grenache, Syrah, Mourvedre and Carignan grapes that are meticulously farmed and sorted so only the finest grapes • 2015 Cigalus Blanc, $45 This powerful white wine is made from an unusual mix of Chardonnay, Viognier and Sauvignon Blanc. The Vigonier gives the lovely floral nose, the Chardonnay the body, and the Sauvignon the freshness and acidity. They come together in the mouth to form a harmonious wine with great power and length. Very creative effort. • 2013 Grand Terroir Tautavel, $20 This region in Roussillon near the Spanish border is an up and coming one and Bertrand has a contract for most of the area’s grapes. The wine is medium bodied with a wild earthy nose the French call “Garrigue”, which basically means scrub brush. It has plum and cassis notes on the palate with a clean balanced finish. Very easy to drink and a great partner to grilled chicken. • 2013 Terroir Minervois, $21 (BEST VALUE) This wine stole my heart and made a lasting impact. It is bigger and richer than the Tautavel and is jam packed with blackberry and blueberry fruit with layers of spices and earth mixed in. Made Gerard Bertrand’s Minervois is an outstanding wine as well as a great value. go into the bottle. It is incredibly powerful and yet refined at the same time, with layers upon layers of flavors and a long, lingering finish. Absolutely superb. articles.text: When people hear the term “Great Pacific Garbage Patch,” the image that comes to mind is an endless island of plastic bottles, bags, and garbage. Actually, the Patch is primarily made up of small pieces of plastic, known as microplastics. Unfortunately, the prefix “micro” doesn’t begin to cover the macro effect these materials can have on the environment and our bodies. They are tiny, they are ubiquitous, and they are mysterious. Technically, microplastics qualify as any piece of plastic that is less than 5 mm in length. Despite their inauspicious name, microplastics are the most common source of pollution in bodies of water. Since mass production began in the 1950’s, over 8 billion tons of plastic have been created. About 8 million tons a year end up in oceans. Plastics don’t break down easily like organics do. Microplastics generally start out as larger plastics which gradually break down over time into smaller and smaller pieces. These microplastics stay in the environment unless they are consumed by an organism. Microplastics are in everything. Microplastics can be found in every living organism on the planet and in drinking water sources. Humans ingest them every day in food and water. The average person eats over 40 pounds of plastic over their lifetime, the vast majority of that being microplastics. This is largely due to how common plastics have become. The average American throws away almost a pound of plastic per day. Plastics are used to wrap and package foods, make clothing, and as a lightweight and sturdy shipping material. Plastics have become a cornerstone of worldwide trade, with the top 50 plastics companies conducting over $1 trillion in sales each year. Microplastics accumulate in larger organisms due to the nature of the food chain. Thus, consumers (people) tend to eat a lot more plastic than other organisms. The mysterious part of all this is nobody can say for certain what the health effects are of all this plastic. Plastic molecules are “endocrine disruptors,” meaning that they can mimic and disrupt human hormones. The issue of plastics is not black and white. articles.text: Norma Cadenasso, a longtime member of the Piedmont Seniors group, passed away peacefully on February 22, 2021 after 95 years of a life well spent. Born on November 16, 1925, Norma was the daughter of Peter and Esther Crestetto and younger sister to Ernestine Crestetto McCart. Norma graduated from Piedmont High School, UC Berkeley and the UCSF School of Nursing. As a Registered Nurse, she worked at the Alameda and Oakland Unified School Districts for many years. Her chosen career suited her well given her kind nature, positive attitude, and concern for the well-being of others. She met her loving husband Gene at a church function in Oakland and they spent over 49 wonderful years together, including traveling the world. They particularly enjoyed touring Italy and exploring their family’s origins. Another favorite vacation spot was spending summers at Lake Tahoe, where relatives and friends gathered for endless hours on the beach in conversation, laughter, and marveling at nature’s beauty. Norma also had a number of interests. She was a long-time member of the Bellevue Club in Oakland where she made numerous lasting friendships, played bridge, and shared many joyful occasions with her mother and sister Ernestine. As a member of the Oakland Lawn Bowling Club, she became a skilled player who participated in various tournaments involving other clubs. She Longtime Piedmont resident Norma Cadenasso died on February 22 at age 95. primarily enjoyed it for the camaraderie and opportunity to meet others. She was a member of the Alpha Delta Pi sorority. As a lover of animals, upon retirement she volunteered at the local SPCA where she spent many enjoyable hours exercising the dogs. She also had a strong bond with her pet cat, Peanut, who was often purring comfortably on her lap while she read one of her favorite mystery novels. Even when deer would visit the backyard of her home and make a snack of her roses, she would always greet them with an affectionate gaze. articles.text: If you own a small business, you typically don’t get a lot of recognition, so you may be pleased to learn that March 29 is National Mom and Pop Business Owners Day. You might not necessarily think of your business as a “Mom and Pop” operation, but it certainly contributes to the well-being of your family now, and possibly to that of future generations, too – if you make the right moves. Depending on the nature of your business, you may have spent the past several months more concerned about today than tomorrow, given the serious economic repercussions of the COVID-19 pandemic, which is still placing stress on a great many business owners across the country. If your business has been adversely affected by the pandemic, you might be eligible for a Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan. As you may know, recent legislation provided $285 billion more for this program. To learn more, and to start the application process, visit the Small Business Administration website at www.sba.gov. You have until March 31 to apply for a PPP loan. Other relief also may be available. But regardless of whether you apply for one of these loans, you can take other steps to help maximize the benefits you get from your business – and perhaps even extend its longevity.
