Business owners’ issues go beyond ‘mom and pop’ label If you own a small business, you typically don’t get a lot of recognition, so you may be pleased to learn that March 29 is National Mom and Pop Business Owners Day. You might not necessarily think of your business as a “Mom and Pop” operation, but it certainly contributes to the well-being of your family now, and possibly to that of future generations, too – if you make the right moves. Depending on the nature of your business, you may have spent the past several months more concerned about today than tomorrow, given the serious economic repercussions of the COVID-19 pandemic, which is still placing stress on a great many business owners across the country. If your business has been adversely affected by the pandemic, you might be eligible for a Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan. As you may know, recent legislation provided $285 billion more for this program. To learn more, and to start the application process, visit the Small Business Administration website at www.sba.gov. You have until March 31 to apply for a PPP loan. Other relief also may be available. But regardless of whether you apply for one of these loans, you can take other steps to help maximize the benefits you get from your business – and perhaps even extend its longevity. Here are a few suggestions: • Establish a retirement plan. If you don’t already have a retirement plan, it’s never too late to set one up. As a business owner, you have several options, including an “owner-only” 401(k), a SIMPLE IRA and a SEP-IRA. All these plans are fairly easy to establish and can offer potential tax advantages, as well as providing you with a source of retirement income in the future. You may want to work with a financial professional to pick the right plan for your needs. • Coordinate your business assets with your investment portfolio. Like most business owners, you may have a great deal of your personal wealth tied up in your business. And, as the past year has certainly shown, this can be risky. Consequently, you’ll need to weigh this risk factor when deciding on investing in your retirement plan or in other investment accounts. This doesn’t mean you should try to avoid all risk only by pursuing the most conservative vehicles – which would be counterproductive to achieving enough growth to meet your retirement income goals – but you will need to pay close attention to your investment mix to ensure it provides you with an appropriate balance to what you’ve invested in your business. • Develop a transition strategy. How will you make the transition from business owner to the next phase of your life? Will you sell the business outright? Will you gradually transfer it to a family member? If so, what mechanism will you use? It’ a good idea to have these types of plans in place well before you need to enact them, so you may want to consult with your financial, legal and tax advisors soon. March 11, 2021 marked the one-year anniversary of the World Health Organization’s declaration of COVID-19 as a global pandemic. Although the seasons have changed four times since then, I feel as though we have experienced a year-long winter. Winter is often viewed as a time of waiting and the pandemic has forced us into a time of stillness and a slower pace. With vaccinations, the sharp decline in COVID-19 cases has resulted in our lives slowly returning to normal. It seems that we are experiencing a fresh new beginning. In this extralong transition from winter into spring, there are “green shoots” representing new and positive changes everywhere - if you look for them. These changes are noticeable here at The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living community. Our residents, now fully vaccinated, are free to walk around mask-free within our community. They are able to engage with one another with ease and I can once again see the smiles on their faces. Following current CDC guidelines, our exercise teachers, art instructor and choir director have all returned, vaccinated and wearing masks. We had our first live music performance for residents in over a year and masked-up families and friends are visiting again. It feels great! The biggest and most welcomed change is in our beautiful restaurant, The Terrace Room. No longer restricted to having only two persons per table behind a plastic barrier, residents are happy to sit together in small groups and socialize. One resident said that “along with enjoying the great food here, being able to share a meal with others completes the perfect dining experience.” “The timing for the change couldn’t be better,” said Executive Chef Michael Cook. “Our favorite produce company’s sales rep always says that asparagus is the harbinger of spring, and I couldn’t agree more. It’s always great to incorporate locally grown fruits and vegetables into the menu, so I look forward to spring.” Choosing the right produce is an important part of healthy eating for older adults, and Chef Michael knows what to look for. Of the abundance of newly grown spring greens, he said, “You can’t eat enough of them. They provide you with a seriously useful amount of vitamin C to support your immune system and vitamin K to build bone strength. And don’t forget about fresh fruit, especially strawberries,” Michael added while holding up a plump, dark red berry. “These little guys are known to protect your heart, lower your blood pressure and are filled with antioxidants.” For many, food is a source of joy – and one that can help us live life at its fullest. Judy, a resident, said, “Tuesday is my favorite day in The Terrace Room. It means a new lunch menu for the week and a special salad creation. Last week we were treated to a Chef Michael original: poached salmon on a bed of quinoa with cucumbers and asparagus with a Meyer lemon aioli dressing. It was outstanding. I can’t wait to see what he does next.” As we slowly emerge from this year-long winter, I know we will continue to see positive changes. No matter how long the winter, we can celebrate the coming of spring knowing that family, friendship and good food are sure to follow. Dear MacMama: I just got a new MacBook Air, that is still in the box. I am trying to decide if I should transfer all of my files with Time Machine or just start fresh? I have years of stuff that I don’t use, and I started to have some trouble opening some of my files. Also, some of my applications (on my old laptop) have been shutting down unexpectedly. All I really do these days is use my email, write a few Word files, and take photos. My email is through Gmail. The salesperson at Best Buy suggested that I use Dropbox or iCloud to store and transfer my files. Can you explain how that would be different than transferring everything with Time Machine? -Lissa M., Oakland Dear Lissa: This is a great question, and it’s your second sentence that leads me to my answer. Since you are having some application crashes and also have a ton of old files you don’t need, I would recommend setting this up as a new machine. That being said, it would also be possible and even desirable to use Dropbox or iCloud to transfer the files you do want. If you only have a few files that you want to keep (less than a gigabyte or so), I would recommend moving them to a folder in Dropbox before you set up your new Mac. Dropbox is a cloud service. You can think of it as a virtual hard drive. You must have an account, and most likely if you’re going to use it to sync files you already have on your computer, you’re going to want one of their paid accounts. You download the application, sign into your account, and then you would have a folder in finder called, “Dropbox”. Anything that you move into Dropbox; folders, files, pictures, etc. can be synced with other machines that are signed into the same Dropbox account. This gives you the most control over what you want to move over to the new machine. You could create a folder on the desktop of your old machine, called something like “To Be Transferred” or “Keepers”. Then you would simply upload that folder to Dropbox, which is as simple as dragging to the Dropbox icon in Finder. There are plenty of tutorials online about using this application, and their website, www. dropbox.com has very good ones. The nice thing about this is that you can cherry pick things to move over. If you use iCloud to sync your desktop and documents, it will sync everything on your desktop and documents. Anything you don’t want to be stored in iCloud, you have to move out of your documents folder and off of your desktop. This system is great if you want everything to look the same on more than one machine, but not practical if you only want to move a few files over. In your situation, I think Dropbox makes more sense. As far as your photos go, if you haven’t already, I would enable iCloud Photos to sync on your laptop as well as your phone before you set up the new machine. This way, when you sign into iCloud on your new Air, and enable iCloud Photos, all of your photos will come into your photo library. If you have tens of thousands of photos, then make sure to do this well enough ahead of time that the complete library has a chance to upload to iCloud. Since you use Gmail, when you set your email up on the new machine, everything that’s on Gmail’s servers will come into your mail application, so that’s no problem. What won’t come over are any emails you are saving locally, that means folders stored under “On my Mac” in Apple Mail. If this is the case, re-create these folders under Gmail in the folders list in Mac mail, and copy any of the emails in the local folders to Gmail ones. Again, there are lots of tutorials online about how to do this. Here is what makes all of this different than using your Time Machine back up drive to transfer your data. When you use Time Machine, it copies everything on your current computer every hour onto an external drive. This includes everything you see, like documents, files, folders, pictures, your music and photo library, all of your applications, as well as things you don’t see, like preferences, drivers, and files that live in the user and system library. So, if one or more of those files are corrupt, Time Machine still copies it. If you migrate these files to a new computer, it is possible you will inherit any problems you had on your old machine. For this reason, in your case, I would recommend the Dropbox solution. Personally, I use a combination of iCloud and Dropbox. And of course, if you need help, you can contact me, and I can help with the new set-up. For grandparents who live geographically close enough to their grandchildren to see them often, the opportunity to thrive in their roles is great. They’re more likely to understand their adult children’s daily lives and can see where they might be needed to pitch in with the grandchildren. During caregiving, a grandparent builds intimate bonds with their grandchildren. These are also the moments when grandparents can find ways to achieve their self-concept of valued family elder. In 2002 Dr. Arthur Kornhaber wrote The Grandparent Guide – The Definitive Guide to Coping with the Challenges of Modern Grandparenting. He begins his book by asking the reader to think about the many roles that grandparents play for grandchildren, the family, and society. Grandparent roles serve different many functions. At times you may be a nurturer, mentor, or teacher. Other times you will serve as a buddy, hero, role model, spiritual guide, or historian. While one role or another may feel most comfortable for you, no doubt you’ll find yourself from time to time occupying a less familiar function. So, is there really one version of the ideal grandparent? Of course not. Families are unique. But parents and grandparents can align their visions of the ideal grandparent with the right intention. With common sense and mutual respect, families can come up with a shared concept of the role that grandparents will play in their own family. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides, counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com.

articles.text: With registration now open, the Stagebridge Spring Online Performing Arts Institute, or PAI, is a true return to form with beloved instructors exploring the world of Broadway & beyond. articles.text: Caregiving is about more than just one person fulfilling a list of tasks; it’s about human relationships and connection. When someone is looking for home care services for a loved one or themselves, they might be in need of help with bathing, dressing, assistance with using the toilet, medication reminders, meal preparation, or transportation. Professional caregivers receive hours of training so that they can specialize in everything from proper lifting techniques to dementia care at different stages of the disease. Caregiver training, assistance with activities of daily living, and meeting the needs of clients are top priorities, but that is not everything. When a call comes in for a caregiver, a process begins to find a suitable match. In addition to the physical and practical services needed, questions may be asked about personal preferences, unique history, and simple pleasures. This approach to care is to get to know each individual beyond their diagnosis so that they can be expertly paired with a caregiver with whom they can develop a bond, trust, and even true companionship. It’s these connections between clients and caregivers that take home care to the next level, where a spark happens, and two people can get fired up about their common backgrounds or shared interests. These connections lead to more laughter, more smiles, and a caregiver-client relationship that is more than daily tasks and changes in abilities for someone. Whether someone is receiving 24/7 care or just a couple of hours per week, how they connect with their caregiver can have an impact on their overall well-being. But don’t think that this is all about what the caregiver does. Many touching stories of a perfect match are about the client teaching the caregiver something new, such as knitting, playing the piano, or going fishing. These dynamics can reinforce the notion that everyone has something to share, and they are in a care partnership together. By Cynthia Kane Part 4 in a series When young parents and grandparents are asked “What three words would you use to describe the ideal grandparent?” their responses are pretty similar: loving, supportive, patient. New parents want the support of the grandparents, and hope that grandparents will be affirming, respectful, and non-judgmental. Grandparents know this. Books, articles, and websites caution the newest grandparent to “Zip the lip!”, “Follow the parents’ instructions”, “Be a listener”, “Don’t give any unsolicited advice”. Becoming an ideal grandparent in the eyes of your children and grandchildren may well include all of these behaviors, and yet, grandparents have their own vision of their role in the family. According to a 2018 AARP survey, 81% of grandparents polled believe they play a strong role in their grandchildren’s lives. Grandparents do see themselves as caregivers, but they also see themselves as much more. While over a third of those surveyed describe having a role as caregiver/babysitter for young grandchildren, additionally, they see themselves as a source of wisdom and morals, a valued elder, a storyteller, teacher, and conveyor of family history and lore. For grandparents who live geographically close enough to their grandchildren to see them often, the opportunity to thrive in their roles is great. They’re more likely to understand their adult children’s daily lives and can see where they might be needed to pitch in with the grandchildren. During caregiving, a grandparent builds intimate bonds with their grandchildren. These are also the moments when grandparents can find ways to achieve their self-concept of valued family elder. In 2002 Dr. Arthur Kornhaber wrote The Grandparent Guide – The Definitive Guide to Coping with the Challenges of Modern Grandparenting. He begins his book by asking the reader to think about the many roles that grandparents play for grandchildren, the family, and society. Grandparent roles serve different many functions. At times you may be a nurturer, mentor, or teacher. Other times you will serve as a buddy, hero, role model, spiritual guide, or historian. While one role or another may feel most comfortable for you, no doubt you’ll find yourself from time to time occupying a less familiar function. So, is there really one version of the ideal grandparent? Of course not. Families are unique. But parents and grandparents can align their visions of the ideal grandparent with the right intention. With common sense and mutual respect, families can come up with a shared concept of the role that grandparents will play in their own family. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides, counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com. articles.text: Piedmont Recreation Supervisor Erin Rivera announced her retirement yesterday, March 30. Rivera joined the Piedmont Recreation Department (PRD) in 1993 as the Wildwood Schoolmates Site Coordinator and was promoted to Recreation Supervisor three years later. She has served in that capacity for 27 years. During her tenure, Rivera supervised pre-school and elementary school-aged programming, including the Schoolmates program. The city also credits Rivera with growing the department’s preschool programs from an enrichment program into a full preschool program, offering six classes five days a week. “Erin has dedicated her entire career to the Piedmont Recreation Department,” said her boss, Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. “She is responsible for building PRD’s wonderful Schoolmates, Preschool, and camp programs. Her creativity, dedication and service to the Piedmont community has been a cornerstone in the success of the Department for the past 27 years.” Rivera worked to expand the city’s offerings of summer programming as well. She lists Camp Cottontail, Camp Ishi, Camp 1973, Huckleberry, Outdoor Explorers, and Camp Everything as her favorites. She added that she is most proud of the CIT and Junior CIT programs, created in 1995, that have helped match thousands of youth with summer employment opportunities. “I have had the opportunity to work with amazing people over the last 27 years, and we were all always focused on the same goal of providing care and experiences that were good for kids,” Rivera said. “Erin’s enthusiastic dedication to providing great programs that were good for kids has been evident to me since my first day as Recreation Director,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said. “She deserves tremendous credit for the programs she developed and the experiences she’s given to kids in her nearly three decades of work at the Recreation Department.”
